Project Python Foundations: FoodHub Data Analysis¶

Context¶

The number of restaurants in New York is increasing day by day. Lots of students and busy professionals rely on those restaurants due to their hectic lifestyles. Online food delivery service is a great option for them. It provides them with good food from their favorite restaurants. A food aggregator company FoodHub offers access to multiple restaurants through a single smartphone app.

The app allows the restaurants to receive a direct online order from a customer. The app assigns a delivery person from the company to pick up the order after it is confirmed by the restaurant. The delivery person then uses the map to reach the restaurant and waits for the food package. Once the food package is handed over to the delivery person, he/she confirms the pick-up in the app and travels to the customer's location to deliver the food. The delivery person confirms the drop-off in the app after delivering the food package to the customer. The customer can rate the order in the app. The food aggregator earns money by collecting a fixed margin of the delivery order from the restaurants.

Objective¶

The food aggregator company has stored the data of the different orders made by the registered customers in their online portal. They want to analyze the data to get a fair idea about the demand of different restaurants which will help them in enhancing their customer experience. Suppose you are hired as a Data Scientist in this company and the Data Science team has shared some of the key questions that need to be answered. Perform the data analysis to find answers to these questions that will help the company to improve the business.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different data related to a food order. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

Data Dictionary¶

  • order_id: Unique ID of the order
  • customer_id: ID of the customer who ordered the food
  • restaurant_name: Name of the restaurant
  • cuisine_type: Cuisine ordered by the customer
  • cost_of_the_order: Cost of the order
  • day_of_the_week: Indicates whether the order is placed on a weekday or weekend (The weekday is from Monday to Friday and the weekend is Saturday and Sunday)
  • rating: Rating given by the customer out of 5
  • food_preparation_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the restaurant to prepare the food. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the restaurant's order confirmation and the delivery person's pick-up confirmation.
  • delivery_time: Time (in minutes) taken by the delivery person to deliver the food package. This is calculated by taking the difference between the timestamps of the delivery person's pick-up confirmation and drop-off information

###This code cleans the 'rating' column by replacing 'not given' entries with NaN, and converting rating values to numerical variable unlike object type for further EDA
# Replace 'Not given' with NaN and convert the 'rating' column to numerical variable namely float
data['rating'] = data['rating'].replace('Not given', np.nan)
data['rating'] = pd.to_numeric(data['rating'])

# Check the unique values and data type after conversion
print("Unique values in 'rating' after treatment:", data['rating'].unique())
print("Data type of 'rating' after treatment:", data['rating'].dtype)

Unique values in 'rating' after treatment: [nan  5.  3.  4.]
Data type of 'rating' after treatment: float64

Observations:¶

Columns order_id, customer_id, restaurant_name, cuisine_type, cost_of_the_order, day_of_the_week, food_preparation_time, delivery_time contain valid values upon extracting their unique entries. These columns appear to be identifiers with no missing or placeholder values.

Column rating contains the string value 'not given', which indicates that ratings were not provided by some customers who placed orders. This suggests the presence of missing values in the rating column, represented as a placeholder string rather than standard NaN.

To ensure consistent handling of missing data, we are treating 'not given' as a missing value by converting it to NaN using the na_values parameter during data import. This allows us to apply standard missing value detection and imputation techniques.

# This code finds the minimum, average, and maximum time (in minutes)
# it takes to prepare food from the 'food_preparation_time' column.

Minimum preparation time: 20 minutes
Average preparation time: 27.37 minutes
Maximum preparation time: 35 minutes

Observations:¶

The minimum preparation time recorded is 20 minutes, indicating the fastest turnaround for food orders in the dataset.

The average preparation time is approximately 27.37 minutes, suggesting that most orders take between 25 and 30 minutes to prepare.

The maximum preparation time is 35 minutes, which may reflect dishes that requires more preparation time or peak-hour delays.

Observations:¶

Data Analysis Key Findings

Cost of the order: The distribution is right-skewed, with most orders costing less than $20. There are some outliers on the higher end. Food preparation time: The distribution appears somewhat uniform, ranging from 20 to 35 minutes, with no significant outliers.

Delivery time: The distribution is slightly right-skewed, peaking around 25 minutes, with some outliers having longer delivery times.

Restaurant name: There is a large number of unique restaurants, with a few receiving significantly more orders.We have chosen to list the top 20 restaurants

Cuisine type: American and Japanese cuisines are the most popular, while some have very few orders.

Day of the week: Orders are significantly higher on weekends compared to weekdays.

Rating: Among the provided ratings, the distribution is skewed towards higher ratings (4 and 5). A substantial number of orders were not rated.

Question 9: What percentage of the orders cost more than 20 dollars? [2 marks]¶

In [81]:
# This code calculates the percentage of orders that cost more than 20 dollars.
# 1. Filter the dataset to include only orders with 'cost_of_the_order' greater than 20.
# 2. Count the number of such orders and also the total number of orders.
# 3. Compute the percentage of orders above 20 dollars.
# 4. Print the result formatted to two decimal places.

orders_above_20 = data[data['cost_of_the_order'] > 20].shape[0]
total_orders = data.shape[0]
percentage_above_20 = (orders_above_20 / total_orders) * 100
  # Print the result
print(f"Percentage of orders costing more than 20 dollars: {percentage_above_20:.2f}%")

Percentage of orders costing more than 20 dollars: 29.24%

Observations:¶

Order Cost Observation

Approximately 29.24% of the orders in the dataset cost more than $20, indicating that nearly one-third of customers opted for higher-value meals or larger orders.

This insight can help identify pricing trends, customer spending behavior, and potential opportunities for premium deals.

Observations from Multivariate Analysis:¶

Correlation Heatmap:

  • There is a weak positive correlation between cost_of_the_order and food_preparation_time, suggesting that more expensive orders might take slightly longer to prepare.
  • There is also a weak positive correlation between food_preparation_time and delivery_time, indicating that longer preparation times might lead to slightly longer delivery times.
  • There are no strong correlations observed between rating and any of the other numerical variables, which suggests that rating is likely influenced by factors not captured in these numerical columns.

  • Food preparation time vs. Day of the week: Food preparation times also seem consistent across weekdays and weekends.
  • Delivery time vs. Day of the week: Delivery times are generally lower on weekends compared to weekdays, which aligns with the earlier observation about mean delivery times. There are also more outliers with longer delivery times on weekdays.
  • Rating vs. Day of the week: The distribution of ratings seems similar for both weekdays and weekends, with the majority of ratings being 4 or 5.
  • Cost of the order vs. Cuisine Type (Top 10): There are variations in the cost of orders across different cuisine types. Some cuisines like Japanese and American appear to have a wider range of order costs compared to others.
  • Food preparation time vs. Cuisine Type (Top 10): Food preparation times vary across cuisine types. Some cuisines might inherently require more preparation time than others.
  • Delivery time vs. Cuisine Type (Top 10): Delivery times also show variations across cuisine types. This could be influenced by factors like the average distance to restaurants of a particular cuisine or the efficiency of their kitchen.
  • Rating vs. Cuisine Type (Top 10): The distribution of ratings appears similar across the top 10 cuisine types, with most ratings concentrated at 4 and 5, and a notable number of missing ratings for all.

Question 13: The company wants to provide a promotional offer in the advertisement of the restaurants. The condition to get the offer is that the restaurants must have a rating count of more than 50 and the average rating should be greater than 4. Find the restaurants fulfilling the criteria to get the promotional offer. [3 marks]¶

In [88]:
###This code identifies restaurants with over 50 ratings and an average rating above 4 for promotional eligibility.
# Filter out orders with no rating
rated_data = data.dropna(subset=['rating'])

# Group by restaurant and calculate rating count and average rating
restaurant_ratings = rated_data.groupby('restaurant_name')['rating'].agg(['count', 'mean']).reset_index()

# Filter for restaurants that meet the promotional offer criteria
promotional_restaurants = restaurant_ratings[(restaurant_ratings['count'] > 50) & (restaurant_ratings['mean'] > 4)]

# Display the restaurants fulfilling the criteria
print("Restaurants fulfilling the promotional offer criteria:")
display(promotional_restaurants)

Question 14: The company charges the restaurant 25% on the orders having cost greater than 20 dollars and 15% on the orders having cost greater than 5 dollars. Find the net revenue generated by the company across all orders. [3 marks]¶

In [89]:
###This code calculates total revenue by applying tiered surcharges to orders based on their cost.

#Applies the surcharge logic directly to each order.
#Sums the result to get total revenue.
#No extra columns or data modifications—just the final number.

# Calculate revenue for orders > $20 (25%)
revenue_fororders_gt_20 = (data[data['cost_of_the_order'] > 20]['cost_of_the_order'] * 0.25).sum()

# Calculate revenue for orders > $5 and <= $20 (15%)
revenue_fororders_gt_5_le_20 = (data[(data['cost_of_the_order'] > 5) & (data['cost_of_the_order'] <= 20)]['cost_of_the_order'] * 0.15).sum()

# Calculate net revenue
net_revenue = revenue_fororders_gt_20 + revenue_fororders_gt_5_le_20

print(f"The net revenue generated by the company across all orders is: ${net_revenue:.2f}")

The net revenue generated by the company across all orders is: $6166.30

Observations:¶

The company generated $6,166.30 in net revenue solely from surcharges applied to qualifying orders, excluding base order costs.

This figure reflects the effectiveness of the tiered commission model, capturing income from orders above $5 and $20 at 15% and 25% rates respectively.

Question 15: The company wants to analyze the total time required to deliver the food. What percentage of orders take more than 60 minutes to get delivered from the time the order is placed? (The food has to be prepared and then delivered.) [2 marks]¶

In [90]:
#This code calculates the percentage of orders where the combined food preparation and delivery time exceeds 60 minutes

# Count the number of orders where food preparation time + delivery time is greater than 60 minutes
orders_gt_60_minutes_preptime = data[(data['food_preparation_time'] + data['delivery_time']) > 60].shape[0]

# Calculate the total number of orders
total_orders = data.shape[0]

# Calculate the percentage of orders that took more than 60 minutes
percentage_gt_60_minutes_preptime = (orders_gt_60_minutes_preptime / total_orders) * 100

print(f"Percentage of orders taking more than 60 minutes to deliver: {percentage_gt_60_minutes_preptime:.2f}%")

Percentage of orders taking more than 60 minutes to deliver: 10.54%

Conclusion and Recommendations¶

Question 17: What are your conclusions from the analysis? What recommendations would you like to share to help improve the business? (You can use cuisine type and feedback ratings to drive your business recommendations.) [6 marks]¶

Observations:¶

  • The analysis uncovered valuable insights into both customer preferences and operational performance.
  • Weekend orders tend to surge, with American cuisine emerging as the top choice among diners.
  • Shake Shack stands out as the most frequently ordered-from restaurant, indicating its strong popularity.
  • A notable share of orders lack customer ratings, suggesting room for improving feedback collection.
  • Delivery efficiency improves on weekends, with faster turnaround times compared to weekdays.
  • Most orders are fulfilled within an hour, reflecting a generally prompt delivery service.
  • Multiple restaurants qualify for promotional offers, having surpassed thresholds for both rating volume and average satisfaction.

Recommendations:¶

  • Since American restaurants receive the highest order volume, partnering with more highly rated American eateries could further boost customer engagement and sales.
  • To increase orders from underrepresented cuisines such as French, Vietnamese, and Korean, the platform can spotlight restaurants offering competitive pricing and efficient delivery times to attract new customers.
  • Introducing seasonal promotions focused on American cuisine could drive substantial revenue, leveraging its popularity during peak periods.
  • Enhancing delivery transparency by providing real-time order updates can help manage customer expectations and encourage more timely ordering decisions.
